rationale: A wins by keeping its hands cleaner on the facts. Its benchmark angle, "Hugging Face says its 1.8B model rivals one four times its size — and the open weights mean anyone can check," preserves the uncertainty; B's "matches one four times its size" quietly upgrades "near" into a stronger claim. Both sets found the four real shapes, but A is less likely to get the founder embarrassed on a reporter call.
gaps_in_A: "standard launch news" slightly undersells the developer angle; if the model is actually usable offline on phones, that can live longer than a 24-hour launch item with the right demo proof.
"a classic open-core test case" is plausible but a little tidy; the update supports open-source commercialization, not a fully proven open-core strategy.

"zoomed down to one named buyer" leans on the supplied fact that a named Fortune 100 manufacturer exists, but the actual name is absent from the brief; A catches this later, but the headline should not make it feel solved.
gaps_in_B: "matches one four times its size" overstates the supplied fact, which says benchmarks put it near a model 4x its size. That is a small word with a lawsuit-sized appetite.

"The prevailing belief is that reasoning quality tracks parameter count" is imported context, not in the update. Maybe true enough, but this exercise asked for grounded angles, not a TED Talk premise.
"no license fee in a commercial app" is an inference from Apache 2.0, and it needs legal/packaging care before a founder says it out loud.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the first story type; this is business-model/open-source commercialization, not funding. The angle survives, but the label is sloppy.
